on a line from Szymborska My departure from the city of O.? I took no leave. I’d learned to sleep angry. On a train I was contained. The water under the bridge was just that. Shunned metaphor. The world was not too much or too much with me. I stomached it. In the photograph I only look lonely because I was alone. You can imagine it that way. Only none of it was like that, not like that at all.

outputs.L1:
**On a Line from Szymborska**

My departure from the city of O.? I took no leave.
I had learned to sleep in anger. On the train, I was contained.
The water beneath the bridge was only that. I shunned all metaphor.
It sent no waves of regret, nor stirred me to reflection.
It did not baptize, nor wash away, nor cleanse.

The countryside unfolded like the reaches of any country
where rain descends and cattle graze on yellow blossoms.
The world was neither too much, nor too much with me.
I bore it. In the photograph, I appear lonely only because I was alone.
You cannot see the envelope resting on my lap,
nor the letters tucked beneath the sweaters in my suitcase.

I carried but a single bag—only what I could manage in a crowd.
You may imagine I clutched a weighty book
from which nothing could divert me.
You may imagine my head held high, my eyes gone dry.
I did not regard my departure as a failure, nor as a fall.
I had dodged a bullet. I had been reborn.

You may imagine it so.
Only none of it was like that—not like that at all.

---

I preserved every image and idea while refining the phrasing for smoother rhythm and a more elevated tone. If you'd prefer a version that stays closer to the original's spare, understated style (a hallmark of Szymborska's voice), I'd be glad to offer a lighter touch instead.

after Szymborska

Leaving the town of O.? No goodbyes for me. I had taught myself to fall asleep even while furious. Seated on a train, I stayed composed. The river flowing beneath the bridge was nothing more than that. I refused all metaphor. No ripples of remorse came from it, nor did it prompt any pondering. It offered no baptism, no washing clean, no cleansing of the soul. The land outside resembled the edges of any nation—places where rain comes down and cattle munch on yellow blossoms. The world neither overwhelmed me nor pressed too heavily upon me. I simply swallowed it whole. If I seem solitary in that picture, it's merely because no one was beside me. What you can't spot is the envelope resting on my knees, or the notes tucked beneath the sweaters in my luggage. Just a single bag traveled with me, only as much as I could handle amid a throng. Picture me clutching some hefty volume, so absorbed nothing could pull me away. Picture my chin lifted, my eyes without a trace of tears. To me, my leaving wasn't a defeat or a downfall. I had narrowly escaped harm. I had begun anew. You're free to imagine it that way. Except none of it happened so—not in the slightest.

# Leaving O.

I left the city of O. without a single farewell. There was no ceremony to it, no lingering embrace at a doorway, no final glance over my shoulder at the streets I was abandoning. By then I had grown accustomed to sleeping while angry, and departure came to me the same way—quietly, without resolution, the anger folded up and carried off like everything else.

Let me be clear about what I saw as I went. The water was only water. The countryside was only countryside, and the landscape that unrolled past the window was nothing more than a landscape. I refuse the temptation to make these things mean something. The river did not murmur of regret. The open fields did not promise renewal. I know how these stories are supposed to work, how the natural world is meant to mirror the traveler's heart, but I will not offer you that. These were ordinary things, and I insist on their ordinariness.

Understand, too, that I was not swept away by any of it. I did not dissolve into grief or drown in what I was leaving behind. If anything, I stomached the world—I took it in, held it down, contained it. My restraint was not weakness but a kind of discipline. Whatever pressed against me from the outside, I met it with a closed and steady surface.

That surface, of course, concealed a great deal. Behind my composed expression there were things I did not show: an envelope tucked into the lining of my suitcase, letters folded and hidden away, the evidence of a story too painful to display. I carried my history the way I carried my luggage—privately, its weight invisible to anyone who might have watched me pass.

And here is where I might invite you to imagine my leaving as something grand. Picture it, if you like, as a triumphant rebirth, a woman shedding her old life and stepping free into a wider world. Or picture it as a narrow escape, a flight from danger accomplished at the last possible moment. Build whichever version pleases you.

But I should tell you, before you settle too comfortably into either: it was not like that at all.
outputs.L4:
# Leaving Without a Story

The speaker stands at the threshold of departure, suitcase in hand, watching a city recede behind them. But this is no ordinary farewell scene. Where we might expect tears, longing glances, or the swelling ache of nostalgia, the speaker offers something far more unsettling: a flat, deliberate refusal to feel—or at least, a refusal to perform the feeling we anticipate.

Throughout the poem, the speaker resists the temptation to transform their leaving into something poetic. There is no metaphor to soften the blow, no rain falling in sympathetic sorrow, no dramatic gesture to mark the weight of the moment. The streets are simply streets. The train is simply a train. By insisting on this plainness, on the unadorned facts of departure, the speaker seems to be guarding against something—perhaps the very sentimentality that would make the pain legible, and therefore bearable.

And yet, running beneath this surface of detachment is a strange, recurring gesture. Again and again, the speaker invites us to *imagine*: imagine a tender goodbye, imagine a reconciliation, imagine the emotions that ought to accompany such a leaving. These invitations conjure vivid alternative narratives—the comforting fictions we tell ourselves about endings, the tidy stories that give grief its shape and meaning.

But each time, the invitation is withdrawn. The final, devastating turn comes when the speaker denies that anything happened "like that at all." The imagined scenes collapse. The tender goodbye never occurred. The reconciliation was only a possibility we were asked to picture, never a reality we were permitted to keep.

This is where the poem's true power lies. In the space between the comforting fictions and the blunt denial, we sense an enormous, unspoken grief—a loss so real and so unresolved that it cannot be dressed up in the borrowed clothes of sentiment. The speaker's insistence on plain reality is not coldness but a kind of honesty, and perhaps a kind of self-protection. To imagine the story would be to lie; to tell the truth is to admit that nothing was resolved, nothing was healed, and nothing was said that needed to be said.

The poem leaves us in that uncomfortable gap, holding the weight of everything that did not happen. And in doing so, it reminds us how often we reach for narrative to make our losses survivable—and how devastating it can be when someone refuses to let us.
outputs.L5:
# Szymborska and The Shunned

Wisława Szymborska, the Polish poet who received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1996, built her reputation on a poetry of quiet observation, gentle irony, and profound humanity. Across her body of work, she gave voice to the overlooked, the small, and the marginal—those who, in one way or another, might be called the shunned.

## Giving Voice to the Overlooked

One of the most striking qualities of Szymborska's poetry is her willingness to turn attention toward subjects that others ignore. Whether writing about an onion, a stone, a museum artifact, or an anonymous figure lost to history, she elevated the ordinary and the neglected. In doing so, she reminded readers that dignity does not depend on prominence, and that even the shunned—the forgotten, the excluded, the passed-over—carry meaning worth examining.

## The Outsider's Perspective

The theme of the shunned appears throughout her work in various forms. Szymborska often adopted the stance of an outsider looking in, questioning accepted truths and challenging comfortable assumptions. She wrote about victims of history, the anonymous dead of wars and catastrophes, and the countless lives that pass unrecorded. Her poem "The End and the Beginning," for instance, considers those who clean up after conflicts—the unglamorous, forgotten workers whom history tends to shun in favor of heroes and leaders.

## Compassion Without Sentimentality

What distinguishes Szymborska's treatment of shunned subjects is her refusal to lapse into easy sentiment. She approached difficult themes with a light touch, often laced with wit and irony, yet never lost her essential compassion. This balance allowed her to acknowledge suffering and exclusion honestly while affirming the value of every individual existence. The shunned, in her vision, are not merely objects of pity but fellow inhabitants of a strange and wondrous world.

## A Lasting Legacy

Szymborska's genius lay in her ability to make readers see anew. By training her poetic gaze on the marginal and the shunned, she expanded the boundaries of what poetry could hold. Her work endures because it insists on the significance of the seemingly insignificant—an invitation to notice, to question, and to embrace the full range of human experience, including those parts we are tempted to turn away from.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that begins with a line borrowed from Szymborska about leaving the city of O., using her style of understatement and refusing sentimentality.
counterfactuals.output:
**Leaving the City of O.**

*Nothing has happened, nothing that would matter.*
The train pulls out at the usual hour,
neither ashamed nor proud of leaving.

The city of O. does not turn to watch.
It has other windows to be lit in,
other buses to be nearly missed.

I packed the way one packs:
two shirts, a comb, the small arithmetic
of what fits and what gets left behind.

The left-behind does not complain.
A chair remains a chair without me.
The river continues its one idea.

I will not say the streets remembered anything.
Streets are professionals. They forget
the way water forgets the shape of hands.

Somewhere a door I closed stays closed.
This is not tragedy. This is a door
doing the only thing a door can do.

I could invent a last look, a lump
in the throat, a sky arranged for the occasion.
But the sky was merely overhead, as usual,

and the occasion was a Tuesday,
and the city of O., which owes me nothing,
paid in full by letting me go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem about leaving a place behind without emotional farewells, deliberately rejecting metaphors like "water under the bridge."
counterfactuals.output:
# Departure Without Ceremony

I will not call this water under any bridge—
the phrase is tired, and so am I of tired things.
Let me just say: I packed the boxes.
I labeled them in permanent marker.

There was no last long look.
I did not stand in the doorway
letting the light do something meaningful
across the empty floor.

The floor was just empty.
The light was just light.

I don't need a river to explain me to myself,
don't need the current as a stand-in
for whatever it is people feel
when they decide to go.

I turned the key. I heard the lock.
That sound was not a metaphor for closure—
it was a lock, doing its one job,
which is more than I can say for most departures.

The neighbors didn't wave.
I didn't want them to.
I wanted the ordinary fact of leaving
to stay exactly its own size:

a car, a road,
the mirror I refused to check,
and the plain arithmetic of miles
adding up to somewhere else.

Call it nothing.
Call it Tuesday.
I am not the bridge.
I am not the water.

I am just the one who left,
and did not turn it into weather.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person poem in the voice of someone departing a city by train, describing a photograph and what it hides, in the manner of Wisława Szymborska.
counterfactuals.output:
**Departure, With Photograph**

The train pulls east and I hold you
in my lap, a rectangle of stopped weather,
the two of us squinting into a July
that has since agreed to end.

You are laughing in the picture.
The camera believed you.

Behind us, the café awning is striped
and certain of itself.
Nobody photographs what is coming—
the phone call in October,
the way a word can close a door
without touching it.

Look how the light falls on the table.
It does not know it is falling.
The two cups are still full.
We had not yet decided
who would be the one to leave first.

Outside my window now,
a country of fields recites itself,
each identical, each different,
the way days are.

The photograph keeps its one afternoon
the way a fist keeps a coin—
tightly, and for no one.
It cannot show your hands
which I remember better than your face,
cannot show the argument
folded just under your smile
like a letter in a pocket.

I could tell you the whole story.
The photograph would still insist
we were happy,
and it would not be lying,
exactly.

The train goes on being a train.
I put you back into my coat.
Somewhere the café is being torn down
or repainted—
I will never know which,
and this, too,
is a kind of tenderness.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem that repeatedly invites the reader to imagine a scene of resilient departure, then undercuts it in the final lines by admitting none of it was true.
counterfactuals.output:
**Postcard I Never Sent**

Imagine the platform, the whistle, the steam,
the way I squared my shoulders to the wind.
Picture the ticket clenched inside my glove,
the town behind me shrinking to a seam.

Imagine how I did not turn around.
Picture the coat, the collar flipped up high,
the small brave figure walking toward the gray,
each footstep certain on the frozen ground.

Imagine the letter I left on the sill,
the words so calm, so clean, so unafraid—
*I'm going now. I've learned to hold my own.*
Picture the door that clicked. Imagine still

the miles I crossed, the person I became,
the phone I never once picked up to call,
the strength it took to build a life alone.
Imagine all of it. Imagine the flame.

But there was no platform. No coat. No train.
I never packed. The letter stayed unwritten.
I stood at the window and watched the weather change,
and told myself this story in the rain.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a Szymborska-inspired poem about emotional restraint, leaving, and the gap between how a departure appears and how it actually felt.
counterfactuals.output:
**Departure, in Two Versions**

From the outside it was nothing—
a coat, a door, a hand
that did not shake as it turned the latch.
Witnesses, if asked, would testify:
she left the way one leaves a waiting room,
neither early nor late, having read
the magazines already.

But the body keeps a second ledger.
There, the doorknob weighed as much as a planet.
There, the three steps to the street
were a distance measured in decades,
and the coat—the coat was a country
I was being deported from
for crimes I couldn't name.

Consider the economy of it:
how much was spent to appear cheap,
what fortune of restraint
went into the small change of a nod.
The face, that reliable liar,
arranged itself into a Tuesday
while underneath, the sirens.

I have heard that certain stars
went dark a thousand years ago
and only now report their absence.
So with leaving. The eye receives
a calm that isn't there,
a light already contradicted
by the dark that sent it.

What would honesty have looked like?
Perhaps a woman kneeling on a sidewalk,
holding the pavement so the earth
would not tip her off entirely.
Instead: good posture.
Instead: the click of a latch,
that modest, that catastrophic sound.

I offer no apology for the discrepancy.
Between the seismograph and the still room
someone must have chosen the still room.
It was, I think, a kind of courtesy—
to spare the doorway,
to let the ordinary Tuesday
keep believing in itself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
